First lessons and choosing a coach

Many shooters begin with lessons from a coach, a trainer who teaches safety, technique and how to prepare for competitions. Many faults are hard to feel from behind the gun. A coach sees them from the outside and corrects them before they become habits. Changing a habit that has set in usually takes much longer than learning the movement well from the start.

At the first lesson the coach usually starts with safety and gun handling: how to carry, open and load the gun. Then they check your master eye: with both eyes open, one eye takes charge of lining up the barrels with the target, and the coach needs to know which one. After that they show you the stance and the gun mount, the movement that brings the gun to your cheek and shoulder.

The first targets are simple and slow, often going away from you. The aim of the first lesson is to break a few targets safely and enjoy it, not to get a high score. Many grounds lend a gun and sell cartridges for lessons, so you do not need your own gun to start. When to buy one: Choosing your first gun.

In the next lessons the coach checks whether the gun fits you, which is called gun fit. They also help you build a short routine before each shot and choose a way to give the target lead: how far ahead of it you point. The coach keeps an eye on your safety the whole time.

How to choose a coach. Ask about qualifications. In many countries coaches hold a certificate from the national federation or another recognised coaching programme; the requirements differ between countries. Ask whether the coach works with beginners: a strong shooter does not automatically teach well. It also matters that you understand each other, in language and in the way they explain.

Tip: If the coach speaks another language, you can train with an interpreter or agree in advance on a few key words and hand signals. More in Training with a coach who speaks another language.

Think about your discipline. A coach who shoots Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting usually knows its rules and typical targets well. The place matters too: regular lessons near home often do more than rare trips to a ground far away.

Start with a trial lesson. Afterwards ask yourself honestly: did you feel safe, was it clear, do you want to come back? If not, try another coach; that is normal.

You can find a coach at your ground, through your national federation or in the ClayArena coach catalogue, which you can filter by discipline, country and training language (Finding a coach and a shooting ground on ClayArena). Advice from friends is useful, but it does not replace a coach: an experienced shooter may find it hard to explain what they do.

Key points

  • Lessons with a coach build safety and good habits from the first shot
  • First lesson: safety, master eye, stance, mount and easy targets
  • Look for a qualified coach who teaches beginners and explains in a way you understand
  • A trial lesson shows whether a coach suits you
  • Find coaches at your ground, through your federation or in the ClayArena coach catalogue

Did you know?

Many experienced competitors keep working with a coach for years: an outside eye spots small faults that the shooter cannot feel.

For parents
  • For a child, ask whether the coach regularly teaches juniors and how children are supervised at the ground. Ask whether a lighter gun or lighter cartridges are available for a start. More in Safety and supervision.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Why do many shooters begin with a coach rather than teach themselves?

    1. Lessons with a coach cost less than shooting alone
    2. A coach watches safety and catches faults before they set in
    3. The rules do not allow shooting without a coach nearby
    Answer

    A coach watches safety and catches faults before they set in

    Faults are hard to feel from behind the gun, and a habit that has set in takes longer to change than to learn well from the start.

  2. What does a coach usually check at the first lesson?

    1. Your ranking in national competitions
    2. How many cartridges you can carry
    3. Which of your eyes is the master eye
    Answer

    Which of your eyes is the master eye

    The master eye decides whether the gun points where you look. If your master eye is on the other side from the shoulder you shoot from (for example, left eye, right shoulder), the coach suggests a fix. Common fixes are closing one eye or putting a dot on your glasses.

  3. A trial lesson felt unclear and uncomfortable. What do many shooters do next?

    1. Try a lesson with another coach
    2. Give up clay shooting for good
    3. Put up with it and change nothing
    Answer

    Try a lesson with another coach

    Coaches explain in different ways, and looking for one who suits you is normal.
